name: Elfnote / Power Patron
tier: Pre-list elite / among the most represented
how: Elfnote monsters, Medius and Power Patron cards convert compact openings into chains of Synchro and Extra Deck interactions, including lines playable on the opponent’s turn.
why: Elfnote placed 10 builds in Houston’s Top 32 including the runner-up. Its important extender Elfnote Tinia was forbidden on October 19.

name: Light and Darkness Ritual / Dark Magician Chaos
how: Black Chaos, Light and Darkness Ritual and Dark Magician-linked cards form a recursive Ritual-focused engine with multiple directions for follow-up and disruption. Hybrid variants can incorporate Albaz/Branded and Azamina tools.
why: Trevor Parker won YCS Houston with the strategy. Magicians’ Souls was subsequently forbidden; the winning configuration cannot simply be copied into the new format.

name: Angelechy
how: A chess-themed control/Synchro strategy centered on its "Problem," "Strategy Score," and "Opening to e4" cards, supported by high-density hand traps and disruption.
why: Eight Angelechy variants occupied Houston Top 32 places, including a semifinalist and two other Top 8 finishes.

name: Branded / Despia
how: Fallen of Albaz, Mirrorjade and a broad Fusion toolbox turn the Extra Deck into removal, interruption and Grind-game recursion; Dogmatika and Chaos support permit hybrid builds.
why: Reached Houston’s Top 16, but stood below the three dominant families in representation.

name: Yummy
how: Low-Level monsters and compact Synchro routes let Yummy spend more of its Main Deck on proactive disruption and hand traps than many combo decks can afford.
why: A Yummy list reached Houston’s Top 32. Cupsy★Yummy Way was forbidden on October 19, changing the deck’s prospects.

name: Mitsurugi (pure / hybrid)
tier: Historically relevant 2026 engine / below Houston leaders
how: Ritual monsters plus flexible support recycle resources and extend through interaction; the engine also mixes well with other packages, including Chaos Ritual lines.
why: Present at high-level Houston tables and as part of evolving hybrid configurations; it should not be treated as a proven standalone top-six post-list strategy. Ame no Habakiri no Mitsurugi was forbidden.

name: Tearlaments
how: Milling or sending Tearlaments monsters to the Graveyard triggered Fusion Summons by returning materials to the Deck. Its reactive effects converted ordinary setup into pressure on both turns.
why: Tearlaments appeared in 17 of the Top 32 at YCS Minneapolis, including hybrids. The later Ishizu version was far more dominant.

name: Spright
how: Level/Rank/Link 2 monsters such as Spright Blue, Jet, Gigantic Spright and Spright Elf produced repetitive, consistent starters and interruptions while restricting Special Summon choices.
why: Eleven Minneapolis Top 32 lists used Spright cards; two builds combined Spright and Tearlaments.

name: Floowandereeze
how: Chains of Normal Summons, returning banished small birds, and cards like Empen and Dimension Shifter attacked decks that depended on the Graveyard.
why: Three decks made the Minneapolis Top 32. Particularly effective at exploiting Tearlaments matchups.

name: Runick Spright
how: Joined Spright’s Level 2 consistency with Runick Quick-Play Spells and Fountain to gain cards, disrupt actions and banish the opponent’s Deck.
why: An important champion-level combination, with Runick Spright visible in the Minneapolis Top 32. It exemplified the era’s interchangeable small engines.

name: Exosister
how: Punished cards moving out of Graveyards, upgraded Level 4 sisters into impactful Xyz monsters, and could banish opposing cards efficiently.
why: Won a major 2022 YCS and remained a strong response to Graveyard-centric formats; present in the Minneapolis Top 32.

name: Bystial Dragon Link
how: Bystial monsters banished LIGHT/DARK cards from Graveyards while dragon engines linked together extenders, searching and Synchro/Link threats.
why: A Dragon Link list and Bystial-based variations made the Minneapolis top cut, but this family was not as prevalent as Tearlaments or Spright.

name: Thunder Dragon
how: Discard and banishment triggers generated card advantage, while Thunder Dragon Colossus blocked the opponent from adding cards from the Deck to hand except by drawing.
why: Nine of Niagara Falls’ Top 32 lists were Thunder Dragon. The deck checked opponents that relied heavily on searching.

name: Gouki / Warrior Link
how: Gouki monsters replaced themselves through Graveyard searches and fueled Link climbing, Extra Link boards, and at times hand-disruption routes.
why: Eight of the Top 32 at Niagara Falls played Gouki; the runner-up used it. Its oppressive end boards helped define early Link-era design problems.

name: Sky Striker
how: A small engine around Raye and multiple Extra Deck forms, powered by Engage, Widow Anchor and three-Spells-in-Graveyard bonuses.
why: Four Sky Striker decks reached Niagara Falls Top 32 and the archetype won the event, showing that representation and winning are not identical.

name: Danger! Dark World / Burning Abyss
how: Danger! monsters offered reveal-and-discard interactions that often both Special Summoned a body and drew a card, supercharging Graveyard-friendly partners.
why: The official Niagara list contained three Danger! Dark World, two Danger! Burning Abyss and one Danger! SPYRAL lists.

name: Altergeist
how: Trap-centric control around Multifaker, Silquitous and Hexstia repeatedly interrupted opponents while maintaining resources.
why: Two Altergeist decks qualified for Niagara Top 32; a dangerous option for players who preferred reactive duel pacing.

name: Pendulum Magician
how: Heavymetalfoes Electrumite helped convert Pendulum cards into searching, recycling and extra resources for a broad Extra Deck.
why: One Pendulum deck made the Niagara Top 32. Earlier 2018 variants were more prominent than this late-year result suggests.

name: Burning Abyss
how: Dante milled cards to trigger Malebranche Graveyard effects; looping monsters and traps let the deck grind through repeated exchanges.
why: Eleven of the 32 Anaheim decks used Burning Abyss. It remained competitively relevant long after 2014.

name: Qliphort
how: Pendulum Scales repeatedly replaced Tribute material and enabled huge threats such as Apoqliphort Towers, often protected by floodgates.
why: Ten Anaheim top-cut decks played Qliphort, making it the most prominent early Pendulum deck of the period.

name: Shaddoll
how: Shaddoll Fusion punished opponents controlling Extra Deck monsters, while Flip and Graveyard effects rewarded both Fusion Summoning and sending material away.
why: Nine Anaheim Top 32 lists were Shaddoll. El Shaddoll Construct and Winda shaped how players planned their turns.

name: Satellarknight / Tellarknight
tier: Tier 1 early on / still viable late
how: Deneb–Altair loops created recurring Level 4 bodies to make disruptive Rank 4 Xyz monsters, including Triverr, backed by effective traps.
why: Two Tellarknight players qualified for Anaheim Top 32; a measured Xyz-control strategy.

name: Geargia
how: Geargiarmor, Geargiaccelerator and Geargiagear produced repetitive Machine searching and Rank 4 access while sustaining a heavy trap lineup.
why: A major first-half strategy rather than a leading November deck; included to represent the entire calendar year.

name: HAT (Hands / Artifacts / Traptrix)
how: Fire Hand and Ice Hand punished destruction, Artifacts forced reactive interaction, and Traptrix provided searches and Trap Hole lines.
why: A signature adaptable control shell; displaced by the Shaddoll/Burning Abyss/Qliphort rise later in the year.

name: Chaos / Yata-Lock
how: Chaos Emperor Dragon – Envoy of the End, Sangan/Witch and Yata-Garasu could wipe resources and deny future draws; Chaos builds also used Black Luster Soldier – Envoy of the Beginning.
why: A foundational example of why the Forbidden List was necessary. "Yata-Lock" describes a particular lock sequence, not every Chaos deck.

name: Goat Control
how: Scapegoat, Metamorphosis, Thousand-Eyes Restrict and a flexible suite of power spells made a slow, technical resource game.
why: Its strategic depth is still celebrated through Goat Format events; generally not described as a modern-style Tier 0 deck.

name: TeleDAD
how: Emergency Teleport supplied easy Tuners to a Destiny HERO draw engine and Dark Armed Dragon for powerful removal and finishers.
why: Defined a famously expensive and concentrated tournament environment and accelerated the importance of Synchro Summoning.

name: Blackwing
how: Black Whirlwind searched a large suite of self-Special-Summoning DARK Winged Beasts while Icarus Attack controlled the board.
why: One of the key Synchro-era archetypes; fast, straightforward board development paired with strong removal.

name: Lightsworn
how: Milling fuelled Judgment Dragon, Wulf and other powerful finishers; the deck traded perfect consistency for explosive ceiling.
why: A formative high-variance competitive deck remembered for ending games in a rush of board wipes and Special Summons.

name: Frog FTK
how: Substitoad repeatedly sent Frogs to the Graveyard to enable a Mass Driver burn loop that could win on the first turn.
why: Historically important as an FTK engine even though a first-turn kill is not the same as a proven Tier 0 share; Substitoad was forbidden.

name: Infernity
how: Infernity Archfiend and Infernity Launcher rewarded empty hands with chained searches and Synchro summons.
why: An influential precursor to combo decks with enormous first-turn advantage; Launcher restrictions reduced its power.

name: Six Samurai
how: Gateway of the Six and Legendary Six Samurai - Shi En made fast swarms and strong Spell/Trap negation possible.
why: A favorite of the early 2011 championship field and a major test of how much value a repeatable searching card could produce.

name: Plant Synchro
how: Lonefire Blossom, Spore, Glow-Up Bulb and Dandylion enabled multiple flexible Synchro lines from Graveyard-friendly materials.
why: A gold standard for intricate resource sequencing in the 5D’s period; its core remained influential in later combo decks.

name: Wind-Up
how: Wind-Up Magician, Shark, Rat and Carrier Zenmaity converted small openings into Rank 3/4 Xyz and repeated Hunter hand destruction.
why: A defining 2012 archetype; key restrictions targeted the oppressive hand loop.

name: Inzektor
how: Dragonfly and Centipede equipped Hornet to destroy cards, summon or search additional Inzektors and snowball advantage.
why: Feared for converting ordinary engine cards into repeated targeted removal.

name: Dino Rabbit
how: Rescue Rabbit summoned Normal Dinosaurs that became Evolzar Laggia or Dolkka, backed by efficient traps and Tour Guide packages.
why: One of the cleanest examples of an Xyz-era control deck with a compact, reliable opening.

name: Dragon Ruler
tier: Tier 1 and often considered Tier 0-level pressure
how: Blaster, Tidal, Tempest and Redox repeatedly revived or searched Dragons, fuelling Rank 7 Xyz, huge boards and relentless recursion.
why: Defined 2013 alongside Spellbooks. Won the 2013 North American WCQ, and its capacity to rebuild almost indefinitely made multiple waves of restrictions necessary.

name: Spellbook / Prophecy
tier: Tier 1 / opposing pole to Dragon Ruler
how: Spellbook of Judgment could add multiple Spellbooks and summon Jowgen to lock out Special Summons.
why: The archetypal control foil to Dragon Ruler in one of Yu-Gi-Oh!’s most famous two-deck environments; Judgment was forbidden.

name: Nekroz
how: Nekroz of Brionac and Clausolas searched Ritual pieces; Unicore suppressed Extra Deck effects; Trishula punished opposing hands, fields and Graveyards.
why: The important missing deck from the original comparison: 22 of 32 duelists at YCS Tacoma played Nekroz, or 68.75% of the top cut. It is a signature Ritual benchmark.

name: Kozmo
how: Small Psychic pilots tagged out into large untargetable Machines; Kozmo Dark Destroyer and Farmgirl enabled sudden removal and OTK pressure.
why: A high-impact, thematically distinctive deck whose resilience and fast damage kept it in major events well into 2016.

name: Performapal Performage (PePe)
how: Performapal Monkeyboard, Skullcrobat Joker, Pendulum Sorcerer and Performage Plushfire turned destruction into searches, then swarmed Synchro/Xyz material.
why: At YCS Atlanta (Feb. 7), 29 of 32 top-cut lists were Performapal Pendulum variants. An emergency list restricted Plushfire, Damage Juggler and key starters starting Feb. 8.

name: Domain Monarch
how: Ehther and Erebus converted tribute summons into enormous tempo swings while Domain of the True Monarchs could deny Extra Deck plays.
why: A leading foil to Pendulum strategies; nine or more Monarch variants reached the 2016 North American WCQ Top 32.

name: ABC / Union Hangar
how: Union Hangar supplied A-, B-, and C-Piece resources that assembled ABC-Dragon Buster, a quick banishing boss that could tag back into material.
why: One of the most efficient Machine engines of its era and a major post-PePe championship threat.

name: Zoodiac
how: A single Zoodiac monster became several Xyz Monsters stacked one atop another, gaining searches, draws and disruption at little initial cost.
why: A transformative one-card Xyz engine; eleven pure Zoo lists plus a SPYRAL Zoo hybrid reached YCS Denver Top 32 even after Ratpier had been restricted.

name: SPYRAL
how: Double Helix and the "Super Agent" engine repeatedly searched or revived resources, building oppressive Link boards and sometimes denying most meaningful counterplay.
why: An extraordinary 29 of the 32 Top 32 lists at YCS Dallas were SPYRAL (90.6%). One of the clearest documented Tier 0 event snapshots.

name: True Draco
how: Tribute Summoning over Continuous Spells or Traps and the Draco search/draw engine let it use floodgates while maintaining resources.
why: One of the year’s major non-combo competitors, notable for its ability to fight without conventional Extra Deck dependence.

name: Orcust
how: Harp Horror, Knightmare, Galatea and Dingirsu created accessible DARK Machine Link/Xyz resource loops; many other engines could feed them.
why: A quarter-plus of premier-event tops often used Orcust and its hybrids: 12 Orcust variants made YCS Fort Worth Top 32.

name: Salamangreat
how: Gazelle, Spinny, Sunlight Wolf and searchable traps recycled the same small engine across turns, offering reliable interaction and strong follow-up.
why: A relatively accessible tournament staple and defining cyberse midrange deck; one of the four groups in the famous TOSS metagame.

name: Adamancipator
how: Rock Tuners excavated the Deck to Special Summon more Rocks; Block Dragon amplified advantage to set up Synchro/Link boards.
why: A central peak-2020 strategy, especially in remote-play environments; its consistency and end boards prompted major restrictions.

name: Eldlich
how: Eldlich the Golden Lord and recurring Golden Land/Eldlixir traps made a slow, resilient control deck; later builds added Synchro, Dogmatika or other engines.
why: One of the strongest engines of the 2020 era, and an important counterweight to giant combo boards.

name: Tri-Brigade
how: Fraktall, Kitt, Nervall and Revolt used Beast/Beast-Warrior/Winged Beast Graveyard resources to summon Link Monsters and banish enemy cards.
why: Its compact engine partnered with Zoodiac, Lyrilusc and others to anchor many 2021 top-level lists.

name: Drytron
how: Drytron monsters used ATK-based Ritual support to cheat conventional Level restrictions and enabled Herald of Ultimateness or other recurring negation threats.
why: Became a defining example of how a generic Ritual-support system could enable extreme turn-one control.

name: Ishizu Tearlaments
how: Agido/Kelbek milled huge quantities while Keldo/Mudora shuffled Graveyards; combined with Tearlaments’ Fusion triggers to generate huge reactive chains on both turns.
why: At YCS Pasadena in November, 26 of 32 top-cut decks used Ishizu Tearlaments (81.25%). This is a much stronger Tier 0 case than the base October 2022 list.

name: Kashtira
how: Unicorn, Fenrir, Shangri-Ira and Arise-Heart weaponized face-down banishment and sometimes locked Monster Zones.
why: A central 2023 tournament deck: 20 of the Top 32 at the 250th YCS Los Angeles were Kashtira.

name: Purrely
how: Small Purrely monsters converted Quick-Play Spells into Xyz material, building large towers-like threats and repeated draws.
why: A premier efficient-Xyz deck and a major alternative to Kashtira across several banlist cycles.

name: Unchained
how: Destroying its own cards triggered extenders; link monsters could use opponents’ monsters as materials to remove boards while advancing its own plan.
why: Eight Unchained decks made YCS Richmond Top 32, the largest group there.

name: Snake-Eye / Diabellstar
how: Snake-Eye Ash, Poplar and Flamberge Dragon generated strong one-card sequences, moved monsters into Spell/Trap Zones and supplied resilient Fire Link boards.
why: At YCS Raleigh, 20 of the Top 32 decks used Snake-Eye cards across pure and hybrid variants. Dominant, though not automatically a Tier 0 format.

name: Fire King Snake-Eye / Azamina
how: Fire King destruction recursion paired with Snake-Eye/Diabellstar consistency and later Azamina support to create difficult, layered boards.
why: An important hybrid and later-year contender; several Fire King Snake-Eye Azamina decks reached YCS Niagara Falls Top 32.

name: Yubel
how: Yubel forms converted attacks and battle damage into threats for the opponent, backed by modern Fiend combo support and powerful disruption.
why: One of the strongest non-Snake-Eye competitors in the second half of 2024, with five Niagara Falls Top 32 decks.

name: Tenpai Dragon
how: Tenpai used Battle Phase Synchro effects and protection to dismantle established boards and end duels with extraordinary damage.
why: A major exception to modern going-first combo orthodoxy; five Niagara Falls Top 32 lists.

name: Ryzeal / Mitsurugi Ryzeal
how: Level 4 access and Rank 4 disruption mixed with Ritual-engine consistency, creating flexible, repeatable starts.
why: Ryzeal and its variants led many early-2025 fields; multiple Mitsurugi Ryzeal and Fiendsmith Mitsurugi Ryzeal builds made the 2025 NAWCQ Top 32.

name: Maliss / @Ignister Maliss
how: Cyberse Link engines exploited banish-based Maliss effects, combining recursive extension with difficult-to-trade-through interaction.
why: Ten Bystial @Ignister Maliss decks reached the 2025 North American WCQ Top 32; an elite mid-2025 engine.

name: K9 Vanquish Soul
how: Vanquish Soul revealed monster Attributes in hand for tailored interactions, while K9 pieces improved consistency and pressure.
why: Twelve of YCS Vancouver’s Top 32 decks used K9 Vanquish Soul, the biggest grouping at that event.

name: Dark Magician Chaos Ritual
how: Dark Magician and the Chaos Rituals: Ragged Records of Rites finds the Ritual pieces, Dark Magical Curtain and Gaze of Timaeus bring Dark Magician and its Fusions.
why: 8.0% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta), the third most-topped deck, and second at the Santo Domingo Regional after the October 19 list.

name: Chaos Ritual
how: Black Luster Soldier and Black Chaos Rituals with Fallen of Albaz Fusions: Ragged Records and Light and Darkness Ritual into Super Polymerization and Dogmatika boards.
why: 4.3% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won Foggia in September. Called by the Grave and Albion were forbidden on October 19, swapped here.

name: Blitzclique
how: Thunder monsters that Special Summon themselves from the hand by destroying Spells and Traps, backed by Hideout in the Sky, Coulomb and Dogmatika Fusions.
why: 3.7% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta), the sixth most-topped deck.

name: Artmage
how: Artmage and Power Patron Fusions: Quick Effect Fusions from Artmage Power Patron, Pendulum Treasure and Super Polymerization, with Ars Magna Spells.
why: 2.8% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won the South Park Regional after the October 19 list.

name: Radiant Typhoon
how: Wind monsters built around Mystical Space Typhoon: Eldam and Swen summon themselves, and Radiant Typhoon Spells set themselves again when MST destroys them.
why: 2.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won Klein Ronnau and Linz in late October.

name: Sacred Beast
how: Hamon, Raviel and Uria brought out fast by Martyr of the Sacred Beasts, Sacred Beasts Released and the Fiendsmith engine.
why: 2.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); second at Donnezac in September.

name: Lunalight
how: Lunalight Fusions: Gold Leo and Tri-Brigade Fraktall feed Perfume Dancer and Leo Dancer, with Fire Formation - Tenki and Forbidden Droplet.
why: 1.5% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won Footscray in September. Called by the Grave, Triple Tactics Talent and Dugares were forbidden on October 19, swapped here.

name: Mermail Atlantean
how: Atlanteans discard Water monsters for value and Mermail Abyssteus searches them, ending on Poseidra Abyss and Rank 7 Xyz.
why: 1.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won the Burnaby Regional in October.

name: Power Patron
how: Power Patron Pendulums with Medius the Pure and Shade the Obscure, Prohibited Power Patron Portal - Terminus and Pendulum Treasure.
why: 1.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); second at Genova in September. Called by the Grave, Triple Tactics Talent and Albion were forbidden on October 19, swapped here.

name: Magistus Fairy Tail
how: Magistus Spellcasters with the Fairy Tail engine: Spenta searches, Fairy Tail - Luna bounces, and Magistus Fusions and Links protect the board.
why: 1.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); won Amadora in September. Called by the Grave was forbidden on October 19, swapped here.

name: Dracotail
how: Dracotail Fusions from the hand at Quick-Effect speed (Faimena), with the End Dragons and Dracotail Spells and Traps set from the deck.
why: 1.2% of TCG tops in October 2026 (yugiohmeta); second at Belo Horizonte in August.
